nodeData.note: Organic production guides: avocado, macadamia, banana, passion fruit, mango, citrus, coffee, tea.

children.note: Avocado is an evergreen fruit tree from the Americas, now a major export crop in Kenya and a growing crop in India. Organic success rests on three things: perfect drainage against root rot, a thick mulch that feeds shallow roots, and clean fruit for demanding export markets.

Macadamia is a long-lived nut tree from Australia, now a major smallholder crop in Kenya, often grown with coffee. Organic quality depends on controlling bugs and nut borers, collecting nuts promptly, and drying them carefully.

A field guide to growing bananas and plantains organically: clean planting material, heavy feeding with compost and mulch, and prevention of weevils, nematodes, Fusarium, Xanthomonas wilt and bunchy top.
A field guide to organic passion fruit: purple and yellow types, grafting for disease tolerance, trellising, carpenter-bee pollination, and prevention of woodiness virus and Fusarium wilt.

Mango is a long-lived tropical fruit tree grown from Kenya's coast and Eastern region to all of India. Organic success rests on grafted trees, a low open canopy, timed water, weaver ants and area-wide fruit fly control.

Oranges, tangerines (mandarins) and lemons are grafted trees that bear for decades. Organic success rests on clean nursery trees, the right rootstock, good drainage, conserved natural enemies and fast action against greening.
A field guide to growing arabica coffee organically, with a focus on Kenya: resistant varieties, shade, mulching and pulp compost, and organic answers to berry borer, Antestia, CBD and leaf rust.

A field guide to growing tea organically, focused on Kenyan smallholders (KTDA) with notes from India: clones, pruning and plucking, organic nutrition that stops soil acidification, biofertilizers, and organic control of mites and root rots.

nodeData.note: Avocado is an evergreen fruit tree from the Americas, now a major export crop in Kenya and a growing crop in India. Organic success rests on three things: perfect drainage against root rot, a thick mulch that feeds shallow roots, and clean fruit for demanding export markets.

children.note: What avocado is, its races and the varieties that matter for growers in East Africa and India.
Avocado is Persea americana in the Lauraceae family. The fruit is botanically a single-seeded berry, picked hard and ripened after harvest.

manas.q: To which plant family does avocado belong?

children.note: Mexican (cold-hardy, thin skin), Guatemalan (thick, rough skin) and West Indian (tropical lowland) races. Most commercial varieties are hybrids between them; genome work shows Hass carries a large Guatemalan share.

manas.q: Name the three horticultural races of avocado.

children.note: Hass has bumpy skin that turns purple-black when ripe and keeps well in shipping. It is the most traded avocado in the world and the main export variety from Kenya.

manas.q: Why is Hass the leading export avocado?

children.note: Fuerte is a Mexican × Guatemalan hybrid with smooth green skin that stays green when ripe. It is common on older Kenyan farms and in local markets but tends to bear irregularly.
Avocado flowers open as female and male at different times of day. Hass is an A-type and Fuerte a B-type; planting both types in one block improves cross-pollination and fruit set.

manas.q: Which flowering type is Hass, and why plant a B-type nearby?

children.note: Trees are grafted. Seedling rootstocks from local hardy trees are common; clonal rootstocks such as Duke 7 or Dusa were selected for better tolerance of Phytophthora root rot, but none is fully resistant.
In India avocado is grown mainly in the Western Ghats, Coorg, Nilgiris and the North-East hills, largely from seedling or local selections; grafted Hass planting is expanding.
Avocado wants a mild climate and above all a soil that never stays waterlogged.
Grows best in subtropical or tropical highland conditions without frost or hot dry winds at flowering. In Kenya the main areas are the central and western highlands.
Roots suffocate within days in waterlogged soil and then rot. Choose deep loams or well-structured red soils; avoid heavy clay, hardpans and valley bottoms.

manas.q: What single soil property matters most for avocado?

children.note: Prefers slightly acid soil; high-pH or limey soils cause iron and zinc deficiency. Test the soil before planting.
Avocado is among the most salt-sensitive fruit trees. Brown, burnt leaf tips and margins can signal sodium or chloride from poor water or fresh manure.
Wind tears leaves, rubs and scars fruit (an export defect) and dries trees out. Plant windbreaks before or with the orchard.
Most root rot arrives on infected nursery plants or in drainage water — prevention starts here.
In Kenya buy grafted seedlings from KEPHIS-registered nurseries; in India from accredited nurseries. Ask for clean potting media, raised benches and healthy white roots.

manas.q: Where should Kenyan farmers buy avocado seedlings?

children.note: Nurseries treat rootstock seed in hot water and grow it in pasteurised or solarised media mixed with compost and Trichoderma, kept off the ground.
Avocado sunblotch viroid spreads through infected budwood and seed and can cut yields while trees look healthy. Take budwood only from tested, clean mother trees.
On any soil with doubtful drainage, plant on raised mounds or ridges and cut drains so water leaves the root zone fast.

manas.q: Why plant avocado on mounds?

children.note: Dig wide holes, mix topsoil with mature compost, and plant at the same depth as in the pot. Spacing depends on vigour and pruning plan; tighter spacing needs regular pruning.
Old Fuerte or seedling trees can be cut back and grafted to Hass, giving export fruit sooner than replanting.
Feed the soil life under a permanent mulch; avoid pushing growth with heavy nitrogen.
Fruit removes mostly potassium and nitrogen, with some phosphorus, calcium and boron. Base top-ups on soil and leaf tests rather than fixed recipes.
Avocado evolved in forest litter and its feeder roots sit near the surface. A thick, coarse mulch of wood chips, prunings and grass keeps roots cool and moist and boosts soil life.

manas.q: Why does avocado respond so well to thick mulch?

children.note: Apply well-rotted compost or manure on top of the soil under the canopy, under the mulch, split at the start of the rains. Fresh manure risks salt burn.
Grow legumes such as beans, lablab or desmodium between young trees and slash them as mulch. Keep cover away from the trunk.
Small, crinkled, mottled leaves suggest zinc deficiency; poor fruit set and misshapen fruit suggest boron. Organic standards allow mineral trace elements when a test shows the need.
Use living inputs at each stage of the orchard.
Mix Trichoderma and mycorrhizal inoculum into compost-based potting media so roots are colonised early.
Opens the full map on Trichoderma.
Dip or drench the root ball with Trichoderma and Pseudomonas, and add enriched compost to the hole.
Opens the full map on Pseudomonas, Bacillus & Streptomyces.
Twice a year, spread compost enriched with Trichoderma and phosphate- and potassium-mobilising bacteria under the mulch.
Avocado roots have few root hairs, so mycorrhizal fungi help take up phosphorus and water.
Steady moisture without waterlogging is the target.
Water stress at flowering, fruit set and early fruit growth causes heavy fruit drop and small fruit.

manas.q: At which stages is water stress most harmful to avocado?

children.note: Small, frequent irrigations under mulch suit the shallow roots. Wet the whole root zone, not just one spot at the trunk.
Basin flooding and long wet spells around the trunk invite Phytophthora. Check drains before the long rains.
Export markets reject fruit with insect damage or live pests, so monitoring is essential.
Thaumatotibia leucotreta, a moth native to sub-Saharan Africa whose caterpillars bore into fruit.
Small entry holes with brown frass or a resin-like ooze on the skin, rotting inside and early fruit drop.

manas.q: What does false codling moth damage look like on avocado?

children.topic: A quarantine pest for the EU
children.note: FCM has been a regulated pest in the EU region since 2014, so a single larva found in a consignment can block exports.

manas.q: Since when has FCM been regulated in the EU region?

children.note: Collect fallen and infested fruit at least weekly and destroy it by deep burial or sealed bags in the sun. Researchers call sanitation the key control.
Use pheromone traps to monitor males. Organic options include FCM granulovirus, Bt, egg parasitoids (Trichogrammatoidea) and nematodes against larvae in the soil.
Biology and organic control of fruit-boring caterpillars.
Tiny insects such as Scirtothrips and greenhouse thrips that rasp young fruit and leaves.
Brown or grey corky scarring and russet on the fruit skin, and silvery or bronzed leaves. Damage is done on small fruit but shows as it grows.

manas.q: What fruit symptom do thrips cause on avocado?

children.note: Check flowers and young fruit with a hand lens, and use blue or yellow sticky cards. Dust from roads favours thrips and mites.
Predatory mites, Beauveria and neem products, and spinosad where your certifier allows it. Avoid broad sprays that kill natural enemies.
Thrips, mites, scales and mealybugs in depth.
The Oriental fruit fly attacks avocado and is a quarantine concern. Use bait stations and male traps, and pick on time.
Area-wide trapping, baits and sanitation.
Root rot kills trees; fruit diseases spoil export quality.
Caused by Phytophthora cinnamomi, a water mould that attacks thousands of plant species worldwide.
Small, pale, wilting leaves, a thin canopy, dieback from the top, and few feeder roots that are black and brittle. Trees may carry a big crop of small fruit before declining.

manas.q: Name three field symptoms of avocado root rot.

children.note: Swimming spores move in water, soil on boots, tools and vehicles, and in infected nursery plants. Waterlogging and heavy clay favour it.
Drainage, mounds, tolerant rootstocks, thick mulch, compost, gypsum for calcium, and Trichoderma or Bacillus in the root zone.
Opens the full map on Damping-off & Root Rots.
Phosphonate (phosphorous acid) injections are a main conventional tool but are not permitted in major organic standards. Check with your certifier.

manas.q: Can phosphonate injections be used on certified organic avocado?

children.note: Colletotrichum and other fungi infect fruit quietly in the field and show black spots as fruit ripens.
Prune out dead wood, keep the canopy open, pick in dry weather, avoid bruising and cool fruit quickly.
Copper sprays are allowed in organic with yearly limits. Copper builds up in orchard soil, and earthworms avoid contaminated soil.
Fungal leaf and fruit diseases.
Weeds compete for water mainly in young orchards.
Digging under the canopy cuts surface feeder roots and opens doors for root rot. Smother weeds with mulch instead.

manas.q: Why should you avoid hoeing under avocado trees?

children.note: Keep inter-rows as a mown or slashed sward or legume cover; use the cuttings as mulch. Herbicides are not allowed in organic.
Opens the full map on Organic Weed Management.
Fruit must be mature, clean and cooled to reach distant markets in good shape.
Avocado does not ripen on the tree; maturity is judged by a dry-matter (oil) test. Immature fruit shrivels and tastes watery, and Kenya regulators close harvest seasons to stop it.

manas.q: How is avocado maturity measured?

children.note: Clip fruit with a short stem stub, place gently in crates, and never drop or throw fruit. Keep picked fruit in shade.
Remove field heat quickly and ship Hass under cooling. Breaks in the cool chain cause uneven ripening and rots on arrival.
Export packhouses grade by size, skin quality and defects. Scarred or pest-damaged fruit goes to local markets or oil.
Kenya is a leading avocado exporter in Africa; rules and buyers set the standard.
Exporters must be licensed by the Agriculture and Food Authority (horticulture), and each consignment needs a KEPHIS phytosanitary certificate. Farms are registered and traceable.

manas.q: Which Kenyan body issues phytosanitary certificates?

children.note: Main buyers are Europe and the Middle East; China opened to Kenyan avocado in 2022. Each market has its own pest rules and residue limits.
Buyers test for pesticide residues against legal maximum levels. Organic fruit must show no prohibited residues, including drift from neighbours.
Certified organic Hass and avocado for organic oil earn a price premium. Perennial crops need a conversion period (usually three years) before the first organic harvest.
Smallholders can certify together under an internal control system, sharing costs. Participatory guarantee systems serve local organic markets.
Opens the full map on Organic Standards & Certification.

Kakuzi Academy (Kenya) — site, soil and planning choices before you plant.
Olivado — step-by-step grafting in English and Kikuyu.
Kakuzi — converting an old tree to a new variety by grafting.
UC IPM experts — long talk on Phytophthora root rot biology and management.
UC IPM — how to sample thrips on leaves and fruit.
FPC Kenya — FCM biology and management for exporters.
Trusted sources for deeper study.
Botany, races, history and world production.

nodeData.note: Macadamia is a long-lived nut tree from Australia, now a major smallholder crop in Kenya, often grown with coffee. Organic quality depends on controlling bugs and nut borers, collecting nuts promptly, and drying them carefully.

children.note: What macadamia is and the varieties grown in Kenya.
Macadamia belongs to the Proteaceae family and is native to eastern Australia. It is the only widely grown food crop from Australia.

manas.q: Where is macadamia native?

children.note: Macadamia integrifolia (smooth shell) and M. tetraphylla (rough shell) are grown, along with hybrids between them.

manas.q: Which two macadamia species are grown for nuts?

children.note: South Africa has been the largest producer since the 2010s; Australia, Kenya and China are also major producers.
Kenya grows local grafted selections such as MRG-20, KRG-15 and EMB-1, alongside Hawaiian cultivars. Seedling trees vary widely and bear late.
Grafted trees start bearing in about four to five years and can produce for decades, so variety and site choices last a lifetime.
A warm, frost-free, moist climate and deep soil suit macadamia.
Grown mainly in the central and eastern highlands (Murang'a, Kiambu, Embu, Meru) where coffee also grows.
Prefers deep, well-drained, slightly acid soils rich in organic matter. Waterlogging invites Phytophthora trunk canker and root rot.
The wood is brittle and the tree is shallow-rooted, so strong wind breaks limbs and topples trees. Use windbreaks and prune for a strong frame.

manas.q: Why do macadamia orchards need windbreaks?

children.note: Clean, grafted planting material from a known nursery is the best investment.
Buy grafted seedlings of named varieties from registered nurseries; they bear earlier and more evenly than seedlings.
Planting two or more varieties together helps cross-pollination and spreads harvest risk.
Dig wide holes, mix topsoil with mature compost, plant at nursery depth and stake young trees against wind.
Beans and other short legumes can be grown between young trees for food and nitrogen, keeping a clear circle around each trunk.
Macadamia has a special root system, so feeding differs from most fruit trees.
Like other Proteaceae, macadamia forms dense clusters of fine roots that release organic acids to free bound phosphorus.

manas.q: What special roots does macadamia form?

children.note: Proteaceae usually rely on cluster roots rather than mycorrhizal fungi, so mycorrhizal inoculants are not a priority for macadamia.

manas.q: Are mycorrhizal inoculants a priority for macadamia?

children.note: Because cluster roots are so efficient, heavy phosphorus applications are unnecessary and can harm Proteaceae.
Nuts and husks remove mainly nitrogen and potassium. Husks hold much of the potassium, so returning composted husks closes the loop.
Spread compost under the canopy at the start of the rains and keep a mulch layer, while leaving the ground clear enough to collect fallen nuts.
Living inputs from nursery to mature trees.
Mix Trichoderma into potting media and planting-hole compost to protect roots from Phytophthora.
Opens the full map on Trichoderma.
Apply compost enriched with Trichoderma and nitrogen-fixing or potassium-mobilising bacteria under the mulch once or twice a year.
Opens the full map on Potash, Zinc & Sulphur Microbes.
Shells and husks can be turned into biochar. A long-term trial in an Australian macadamia orchard tracked soil and leaf nutrients after biochar.
Water matters most while nuts fill.
Drought during nut growth and oil filling gives small, poorly filled kernels and premature nut drop.

manas.q: When is drought most damaging to macadamia?

children.note: Mulch keeps the shallow roots moist; drip irrigation helps in dry spells.
Bugs and nut borers cause most quality losses.
Shield bugs such as the green vegetable bug and coconut bugs pierce the husk and shell to feed on the kernel.
Damage is hidden until cracking: brown, sunken or pitted spots on the kernel. Heavy early feeding causes young nuts to drop.

manas.q: Why is stink bug damage hard to see in the field?

children.note: Shake sample branches over a sheet in the morning, and crack sample nuts to check for spotting.
African weaver ants (Oecophylla longinoda) prey on bugs; a meta-analysis found ants often reduce pests in crops. Egg parasitoids also attack stink bugs.

manas.q: Which ant helps control bugs in African tree crops?

children.note: Bugs, thrips and mites in depth.
Caterpillars that tunnel through the husk into the nut.
Thaumatotibia leucotreta larvae feed on macadamia among many hosts, as do related nut borer moths.
Small holes and frass in the husk, tunnels into the shell, and young nuts dropping early.

manas.q: What signs show nut borer attack?

children.note: Collect and destroy fallen nuts, use pheromone traps, and apply Bt or granulovirus at egg-hatch. Egg parasitoids such as Trichogrammatoidea help.
Biology and organic control of caterpillars.
Rodents gnaw holes in shells, both on the tree and on the ground. Prompt nut collection and clean stores reduce losses.
Soil-borne and husk diseases are the main concerns.
Phytophthora cinnamomi causes bleeding trunk cankers and root rot, especially in wet, poorly drained spots.
Dark, bleeding patches on the lower trunk, bark that peels to show brown wood, yellowing and thinning canopy.

manas.q: What does Phytophthora trunk canker look like on macadamia?

children.note: Drainage, mulch, compost and Trichoderma in the root zone. Do not pile soil or mulch against the trunk.
Opens the full map on Damping-off & Root Rots.
Fungi such as Diaporthe (Phomopsis husk rot) and Pseudocercospora (husk spot) cause husk lesions and early nut drop.
Brown to black husk patches, sometimes with ring-like fungal spots, and nuts that fall before maturity.
Open the canopy, remove infected fallen nuts and husks, and use copper only within organic limits.
Opens the full map on Blights, Leaf Spots & Anthracnose.
In long wet spells, fungi blight the flower sprays and reduce nut set. Good airflow and pruning help.
Weeds compete and hide fallen nuts.
Keep the area under trees mown or mulched so fallen nuts are easy to find and do not sit in damp grass.

manas.q: Why keep the ground under macadamia clean at harvest?

children.note: Slash inter-rows and use cuttings as mulch. Herbicides are not allowed in organic.
Opens the full map on Organic Weed Management.
Quality is made or lost in the days after the nut falls.
Mature nuts fall naturally. Picking immature nuts gives shrunken, low-oil kernels; Kenya has banned immature harvesting.

manas.q: Why should macadamia nuts not be picked green?

children.note: Collect at least weekly, more often in wet weather, to avoid mould, germination, rodent and borer damage.
Remove husks soon after collection; heaped nuts in husk heat up and go mouldy, darkening kernels.

manas.q: What happens if nuts are left heaped in their husks?

children.note: Dry in thin layers on raised mesh racks in shade with good airflow, protected from rain. Do not dry on bare ground or in hot direct sun.
Store dried nuts in breathable bags on pallets in a cool, dry, rodent-proof store. Heat and moisture cause mould and rancid kernels.
Husks are a rich, potassium-heavy compost material. Compost them hot with manure before use, which also kills borer pupae and husk-rot fungi.

manas.q: Why compost husks hot before using them?

children.note: Processors grade kernels by colour, size and oil content; well-filled, mature kernels float in water while immature ones sink.
Kenya is a major macadamia producer with tight rules on what can be exported.
Sell to processors and traders licensed by the Agriculture and Food Authority (nuts and oil crops). Unlicensed brokers often buy immature nuts.
Kenya has restricted exports of raw in-shell nuts to support local processing, and the rules have changed over time. Check current AFA rules before contracting.

manas.q: Why has Kenya restricted raw macadamia exports?

children.note: Kernels are exported mainly to Europe, the USA and Asia. Buyers test for residues and food-safety contaminants.
Certified organic kernels earn a premium. Groups certify under an internal control system; trees need a conversion period before organic sales.
Opens the full map on Organic Standards & Certification.

nodeData.note: A field guide to growing bananas and plantains organically: clean planting material, heavy feeding with compost and mulch, and prevention of weevils, nematodes, Fusarium, Xanthomonas wilt and bunchy top.

children.note: Banana and plantain (Musa) are giant perennial herbs grown across the tropics as a staple food and cash crop. In East Africa cooking bananas feed millions; in India banana is a leading fruit crop.

children.topic: A giant herb, not a tree
children.note: The 'trunk' is a pseudostem made of tightly rolled leaf sheaths. The true stem is the underground corm, from which suckers grow; each pseudostem fruits once and then dies.

manas.q: What is the banana 'trunk' made of, and where is the true stem?

children.note: A banana stool or mat is the mother plant plus its suckers. Farmers keep one bearing plant and one or two followers so that harvests continue for years.
Edible bananas come from wild Musa acuminata (A genome) and Musa balbisiana (B genome). Dessert Cavendish types are AAA; many plantains are AAB; hardy cooking types are often ABB.

manas.q: Which two wild species gave rise to edible bananas?

children.note: Grand Naine (Grand Nain), Williams and Valery are Cavendish types grown for fresh sale and export. In Kenya they are usually planted as tissue culture plantlets.
Cooking bananas of the AAA-EA group, steamed or boiled as a staple in Uganda, western Kenya, Kisii and the Lake region. Most are susceptible to Xanthomonas wilt and weevils.
Widely grown types include Grand Naine and Robusta (Cavendish), Poovan, Rasthali, Nendran (a plantain for cooking and chips) and Red Banana. Choice depends on region, market and disease pressure.
Variety choice is the first disease control. Gros Michel, Sukali Ndizi and Pisang Awak types are prone to Fusarium race 1, while Cavendish resists race 1 but not Tropical Race 4.

manas.q: Which Fusarium race attacks Cavendish bananas?

children.note: Banana wants warmth, steady moisture, shelter from wind and a deep, well-drained soil rich in organic matter.

Growth is best in warm weather around the high twenties °C. Cool spells slow leaf emergence and bunch filling, and frost kills leaves. In the Kenyan highlands cooking bananas grow more slowly at higher altitude.
Banana has big soft leaves and shallow roots, so it needs regular rain or irrigation all year. Long dry spells give small bunches and delayed flowering.
Large leaves tear and tall plants with heavy bunches topple in strong wind. Windbreak trees, dense planting blocks and propping bunched plants reduce losses.
Loams with good structure and high organic matter suit banana best; a pH of roughly 5.5–7 is ideal. Waterlogging quickly suffocates the roots and invites root rots.

manas.q: What soil condition kills banana roots fastest?

children.note: Most banana problems — weevils, nematodes, Fusarium, BXW and bunchy top — travel in planting material, so clean material is the foundation of an organic plantation.
Never take suckers from a sick or unknown field. Infected suckers carry weevil eggs, nematodes, Fusarium and viruses into new land where they stay for years.

manas.q: Why is clean planting material the first line of defence in banana?

children.note: Plants multiplied from shoot tips in a lab are free of weevils, nematodes and fungi, and virus-indexed batches are free of bunchy top. They grow uniformly and fruit together, which helps marketing.

manas.q: Which pests and diseases do tissue culture plantlets leave behind?

children.note: Lab plantlets are first acclimatised under humid shade, then grown on in nursery bags before field planting. Buy only well-hardened plants with several healthy leaves from a licensed lab.

Young tissue culture plants are tender: plant at the start of rains, mulch, water and protect them from weeds. Because they start clean, soil life and mycorrhiza must be rebuilt around them with compost.
Sword suckers have narrow, sword-shaped leaves and a big corm; they make strong plants. Broad-leaved water suckers have a weak link to the corm and give poor bunches.

manas.q: Which sucker type makes the better planting material?

children.note: If suckers must be used, cut off roots and peel the corm surface until it is clean white, removing weevil tunnels and nematode lesions. Dipping pared suckers briefly in boiling water kills the remaining pests.
A low-cost way to multiply clean plantlets on the farm: buds on a cleaned corm are scored and sprouted in sawdust under a humid chamber. Promoted by ICAR-NRCB, IITA and partners.
Dig large pits and refill them with topsoil mixed with well-rotted manure or compost. Spacing depends on variety, slope and system; high-density blocks need more feeding.
Banana is a hungry crop, especially for potassium and nitrogen. Organic growers feed the soil continuously with compost, manure, mulch and recycled banana residues.
Bunches and pseudostems hold large amounts of potassium, so K is often the first nutrient to run short. Returning chopped stems and leaves recycles much of it.

manas.q: Which nutrient does banana need in the largest amount?

children.note: Fill planting pits with well-rotted manure or compost, then top-dress around the mat in a ring several times a year, ideally at the start of each rainy season.
Chop harvested pseudostems and old leaves into mulch. Never recycle plants with Xanthomonas wilt, Fusarium or bunchy top; remove or bury those on site.
In young plantations, beans, Mucuna or Canavalia between rows fix nitrogen, cover soil and can be slashed as green manure. Keep them clear of the young plant's root zone.
Wood ash, compost from banana residues and naturally mined potassium sulphate (allowed in most organic standards) supply K. Use ash sparingly as it raises pH.
Nursery: mix AMF and Trichoderma into the potting medium. Planting: add Azospirillum, PSB and KMB with compost in the pit. Growing: repeat bio-enriched compost around the mat.
Nitrogen shortage gives pale leaves and slow growth. Potassium shortage shows orange-yellow scorching of older leaf edges, leaves that fold at the midrib and thin fingers.

manas.q: How does potassium deficiency show on banana leaves?

children.note: Opens the general map on arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.
Opens the general map on KMB biofertilizers.
Opens the general map on making compost.
Banana uses much water and its roots are shallow, so moisture and mulch decide bunch size.
Water stress during bunch emergence and filling gives small, deformed bunches. Drip irrigation applies water efficiently to the root zone.
A thick layer of crop residue, grass or banana trash keeps soil moist and cool, feeds soil life, adds potassium and smothers weeds.

manas.q: Name four benefits of mulching bananas.

children.note: Leave a small gap of bare soil around the base of each mat; mulch heaped against the stem keeps it wet and gives weevils shelter.
On heavy or flat land, dig drains or plant on ridges. Standing water for a few days kills roots and favours root rot and nematode damage.
Remove extra suckers so the mat does not compete with itself, and cut dead or diseased leaves. Disinfect tools between mats where wilt diseases occur.
Two below-ground pests, the banana weevil and nematodes, cause the most loss; the banana aphid matters because it spreads bunchy top.
Cosmopolites sordidus is a black beetle whose grubs tunnel into the corm. Plants grow poorly, bunches are small and plants snap or topple; cut corms show dark tunnels.

manas.q: Which part of the banana do weevil grubs tunnel into?

children.note: Use clean or pared planting material, cut harvested stems at ground level, and split or chop old stems so they dry out. Synthetic soil insecticides are not allowed in organic production.
Lay split pieces of fresh pseudostem face-down near mats; weevils gather under them and can be collected every few days. Traps also show how bad the infestation is.

manas.q: How do pseudostem traps work against banana weevil?

children.note: Entomopathogenic fungi such as Beauveria bassiana and Metarhizium infect weevil adults; they can be placed on traps. A lab study also found their volatiles repel weevils.
Opens the general map on beetle pests.
The burrowing nematode Radopholus similis, lesion and root-knot nematodes feed inside roots. Roots show dark purple-black lesions, and plants topple with few roots attached.

manas.q: What do nematode-damaged banana roots look like?

children.note: Start with tissue culture plants or pared, hot-water treated suckers, rest or rotate infested land, and build soil organic matter. Neem cake and nematode-trapping fungi are used in India.
Opens the general map on plant-parasitic nematodes.
Pentalonia nigronervosa forms small dark colonies at the base of the pseudostem and between leaf sheaths. Its feeding is minor, but it carries bunchy top virus.
Opens the general map on aphids and other sucking pests.
Several thrips species scar or rust the peel, lowering market grade. Covering young bunches with bags and removing the male bud reduce scarring.
Fusarium wilt, Xanthomonas wilt and bunchy top cannot be cured once in a plant; prevention, hygiene and fast removal are the organic tools. Leaf spots are managed by deleafing and airflow.
Caused by the soil fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc). Race 1 destroyed Gros Michel last century; Tropical Race 4 (TR4) also kills Cavendish and many other types.
Older leaves yellow from the edges and collapse to hang like a skirt, the pseudostem base may split, and a cut stem shows reddish-brown streaks in the water vessels.

manas.q: What does a cut pseudostem show in Fusarium wilt?

children.note: Spores survive many years in soil and move in infected suckers, soil on boots, tools, vehicles and runoff. TR4 has reached Africa (Mozambique); farm hygiene and clean plants keep it out.

Plant resistant varieties and clean tissue culture plants, avoid moving soil, improve drainage and organic matter. Bio-organic fertilizers with Bacillus, Pseudomonas or Trichoderma give partial suppression.

children.note: Opens the general map on wilt diseases.
A bacterial wilt caused by Xanthomonas vasicola pv. musacearum. First seen on enset in Ethiopia, it exploded in Uganda from 2001 and spread across East and Central Africa including Kenya.
Leaves yellow and wilt, the male bud shrivels, fingers ripen early and unevenly with brown-stained pulp. A cut pseudostem oozes yellow bacterial slime within minutes.

manas.q: Which quick field test points to Xanthomonas wilt?

children.note: Insects carry bacteria from ooze on male flowers; contaminated knives and machetes, infected suckers and animals moving between plants spread it further.
Remove the male bud with a forked stick once the last hand forms, sterilise cutting tools with fire between plants, and use clean planting material.

manas.q: Why remove the banana male bud with a forked stick in BXW areas?

children.note: IITA and partners showed that cutting only the sick stems at soil level, quickly and repeatedly, can restore yields without uprooting whole mats.

links.label: 📄 Bacterial diseases of banana and enset (review, 2017)

children.note: Opens the general map on bacterial diseases.
Banana bunchy top virus is spread by the banana aphid and in infected suckers. It is one of the most destructive banana diseases and is spreading in sub-Saharan Africa.

links.label: 📄 BBTV in Africa and aphid transmission (PLoS Pathog., 2022)

children.note: Dark green dot-and-dash streaks ('Morse code') on leaf veins and stalks, then narrow, upright, brittle leaves crowded at the top. Infected plants rarely give a useful bunch.

manas.q: What are the 'Morse code' streaks a sign of in banana?

children.note: Rogue whole infected mats, first killing aphids on them, replant with virus-indexed tissue culture plants and act as a community, since neighbours' sick plants re-infect fields.
Opens the general map on plant viruses.
A fungal leaf spot caused by Pseudocercospora fijiensis: small streaks become black spots that merge and kill leaves early, so bunches fill poorly.
Cut off badly spotted leaves regularly in wet weather, keep spacing and drainage good and choose tolerant types. Copper is allowed in organic within limits.
Opens the general map on blights and leaf spots.
Banana roots are shallow and spread widely, so weeds compete strongly in the first months.
Mulch and cover crops are the main organic weed tools; once the canopy closes, shade suppresses most weeds.
Hoeing deeply near mats cuts surface roots and opens entry points for disease. Slash or hand-pull instead.

manas.q: Why avoid deep hoeing in a banana plantation?

children.note: Opens the general map on organic weed management.
Careful harvest and handling decide price, especially for dessert bananas.
Harvest when fingers are well filled and the corners become rounded; for distant markets cut a little earlier so fruit stays green longer.
Cut bunches into hands, let latex drain, wash and pack on padding. Bruises turn black and lower the grade.
Bananas ripen after harvest. Ethylene gas in ripening rooms is permitted in organic rules for bananas; traditional methods use closed pits or smoke.

manas.q: Is ethylene ripening allowed for organic bananas?

children.note: Green bananas keep best around 13–14 °C. Below that they suffer chilling injury: dull grey peel and poor ripening.

manas.q: What happens to bananas stored too cold?

children.note: Surplus fruit can be dried, made into chips or flour, and pseudostems give fibre for crafts, so less of the crop is wasted.
Organic bananas are a major organic fruit in world trade, mostly from Latin America; in East Africa and India most organic bananas sell locally.
Dry-climate producers such as the Dominican Republic, Ecuador and Peru lead organic banana exports because fewer leaf diseases make organic easier.
Organic bananas are sold mainly in local and urban markets. Certification follows the East African Organic Products Standard or Participatory Guarantee Systems (PGS).
Certification under NPOP is needed for organic exports; domestic organic sales use NPOP or PGS-India.
Organic buyers test for pesticide residues. Keep buffer zones and records, especially next to conventional farms that spray.
Moving suckers across borders spreads TR4, BXW and bunchy top. In Kenya KEPHIS regulates planting material; buy from certified sources.

nodeData.note: A field guide to organic passion fruit: purple and yellow types, grafting for disease tolerance, trellising, carpenter-bee pollination, and prevention of woodiness virus and Fusarium wilt.

children.note: Passion fruit (Passiflora edulis) is a fast-growing perennial vine from South America, grown on trellises for fresh fruit and juice. Two forms dominate: purple and yellow.
The plant climbs with tendrils and bears fruit on new shoots. Commercial vines usually stay productive for only a few years, mainly because of disease.
Passiflora edulis f. edulis: smaller, sweeter, very aromatic fruit preferred for fresh markets and export. Suited to cooler highlands but prone to Fusarium wilt and nematodes.

manas.q: Which passion fruit form is preferred for fresh export?

children.note: P. edulis f. flavicarpa: bigger, more acidic fruit used for juice. Vigorous, suited to warm lowlands and more tolerant of soil diseases, so it is the usual rootstock.

manas.q: Why is yellow passion fruit used as a rootstock?

children.note: Purple × yellow hybrids combine sweetness with vigour. In Kenya KALRO has released hybrid lines, and in India IIHR released the hybrid 'Kaveri'.
Sweet granadilla (P. ligularis) and banana passion fruit (P. tripartita / mollissima) are related highland crops with similar care.
Each flower opens only once. Purple forms open in the morning, yellow forms around midday or afternoon, so pollinators must visit on that day.

manas.q: How long does a passion fruit flower stay open?

children.note: Passion fruit likes mild warmth, steady moisture, sun and free-draining soil.
Purple passion fruit grows best in cooler mid- to high-altitude areas; yellow and hybrid types are planted in warm lowlands such as coastal and eastern Kenya.
Needs well-spread rainfall or irrigation. Long wet, humid spells raise leaf and fruit diseases; dry spells cause flower and fruit drop.
Strong winds damage vines and trellises, so use windbreaks. Frost kills young vines.
Deep, light loams rich in organic matter with pH about 5.5–7 suit it. Waterlogged soil is the main trigger of collar rot and wilt.

manas.q: What soil condition most often kills passion fruit vines?

children.note: Healthy, grafted seedlings from a clean nursery are the best protection against wilt and woodiness virus.
Buy from nurseries certified by KEPHIS or recommended by KALRO. Seedlings can already carry woodiness virus, so avoid roadside or unknown sources.

manas.q: Why buy passion fruit seedlings only from certified nurseries?

children.note: Take seed from ripe, healthy yellow fruits, ferment the pulp for a few days to free the seeds, wash, dry in shade and sow in sterile media.
A purple scion is grafted onto a yellow rootstock, usually by cleft (wedge) graft when stems are pencil thick. The yellow roots resist Fusarium and nematodes better.

manas.q: What is grafted onto what in passion fruit?

children.note: Make the graft well above the soil and keep the union above ground at planting, so the purple scion cannot root into infected soil.
Remove the tape when the union has healed and break off any shoots from the rootstock, which would otherwise outgrow the scion.
Dig wide holes and refill with topsoil mixed with well-rotted compost or manure. Plant at the start of the rains next to the trellis posts.
Dip seedling roots in a slurry of Trichoderma and mycorrhizal inoculum with compost before planting, to protect roots from the first day.
Vines must be trained on a strong trellis; good training gives more fruit, better airflow and easier picking.
The common system: strong posts with one or two wires at about head height. Fruit-laden vines are heavy, so posts and anchors must be sturdy.
T-bar and overhead (pergola) systems spread the canopy wider; they cost more but can carry more fruit.
Grow a single stem up a string to the wire, then pinch the tip to make two arms along the wire. Side shoots hang down as a curtain and carry the fruit.
Flowers form on new shoots, so pruning to encourage fresh growth increases yield.

manas.q: On which shoots does passion fruit bear?

children.note: Prune after the main harvest, removing dead, tangled and diseased shoots. Disinfect knives between plants because sap carries woodiness virus.

manas.q: Why disinfect pruning tools in passion fruit?

children.note: Fruit set and fruit size depend on good pollination: more pollen grains give more seeds, more pulp and heavier fruit.
Large carpenter bees (Xylocopa) are the main effective pollinators: they are big enough to touch the anthers and stigmas as they feed.

manas.q: Which insects are the main pollinators of passion fruit?

links.label: 📄 Pollinator efficacy in yellow passion fruit (Neotrop. Entomol., 2021)

children.note: Honeybees often collect pollen without touching the stigmas, so they pollinate poorly and can even remove pollen.
Yellow passion fruit is largely self-incompatible and needs pollen from another plant; purple sets more readily with its own pollen.

manas.q: Which passion fruit form needs cross-pollination?

children.note: Leave dead wood and logs for nesting, keep flowering hedges and avoid sprays during flowering, even organic ones that harm bees.
Where bees are scarce, transfer pollen with a finger or soft brush from flowers of different vines on the day of opening. Rain washes pollen away.
Opens the general map on pollinators.
Passion fruit flowers and fruits almost all year, so it needs a steady supply of nutrients rather than one big dose.
Nitrogen drives new fruiting shoots and potassium fills fruit and improves taste. Too much nitrogen gives leafy vines with few flowers.
Mix compost or manure into the planting hole, then top-dress in a ring around each vine every few months, especially at the start of the rains.
Mulch keeps the shallow roots moist and cool and feeds soil life. Keep it away from the stem base to protect the collar from rot.
Low legume cover crops between rows add nitrogen and protect soil; slash and use them as mulch under the vines.
Seed: coat rootstock seed with Trichoderma. Nursery: add AMF and Trichoderma to the potting mix. Planting: Azospirillum, PSB and KMB in compost in the hole. Later: bio-enriched compost.
Calcium and boron support flowering, fruit set and firm fruit; shortages give poor set and misshapen fruit. Lime, gypsum and compost help on acid soils.
Opens the general map on Trichoderma.
Opens the general map on organic fertilizers.
Even moisture keeps flowers and fruit on the vine.
Water stress at flowering and fruit filling makes flowers and young fruit drop and gives shrivelled fruit.

manas.q: What happens if passion fruit is water-stressed at flowering?

children.note: Drip lines along the row water the root zone without wetting the collar and leaves, which reduces disease.
Plant on ridges or raised beds where drainage is slow; standing water quickly causes collar rot.
Aphids matter mostly as virus carriers; fruit flies, mites, thrips and nematodes damage the crop directly.
Aphids such as Aphis gossypii and Myzus persicae seldom colonise passion fruit, but they pick up and pass on woodiness virus during brief probing visits.

manas.q: How do aphids spread woodiness virus without colonising the vine?

children.note: Remove weeds and old infected vines that host virus, plant tall border crops as barriers and avoid planting next to old orchards.
Females sting young fruit, leaving marks and causing rot or drop. Use attract-and-kill traps and organic baits, and pick up fallen fruit.
Opens the general map on fruit flies.
Broad mites and spider mites cause curled, bronzed leaves and scarred fruit in dry weather; thrips scar flowers and fruit. Conserve predatory mites and use organic soaps or sulphur where allowed.
Opens the general map on sucking pests.
Root-knot nematodes cause galled roots and weak vines, especially on purple roots. Grafting on yellow rootstock and adding compost reduce damage.
Opens the general map on plant-parasitic nematodes.
Woodiness virus and soil-borne wilts and collar rots shorten orchard life; leaf and fruit spots spoil quality in wet weather.
Caused by aphid-borne potyviruses (passion fruit woodiness virus and related ones such as cowpea aphid-borne mosaic virus). It is the main reason orchards decline after a few years in East Africa.
Mottled, crinkled leaves, stunted shoots and small, deformed fruit with a thick, hard ('woody') rind and little pulp.

manas.q: What do woodiness-infected passion fruits look like?

children.note: By aphids, by sap on pruning knives and grafting tools, and in infected seedlings. Seed transmission has not been shown.
Start with clean certified seedlings, rogue infected vines early, disinfect tools, control weeds and replace old orchards. Mild-strain cross-protection is a research option.
Opens the general map on plant viruses.
Fusarium oxysporum causes wilt, and Fusarium solani and Phytophthora cause collar and root rots. Purple roots are most susceptible.
A vine suddenly wilts and dies; the stem base may crack and darken, and a cut stem shows brown streaks.

manas.q: What are the signs of Fusarium wilt in passion fruit?

children.note: Use grafted plants on yellow rootstock with a high union, good drainage, no wounds at the collar and Trichoderma-enriched compost. Remove and burn dead vines.
A lab study found that antifungal peptides (fengycin) from Bacillus velezensis inhibited Fusarium solani from passion fruit; field use is not yet proven.

links.label: 📄 Bacillus velezensis vs Fusarium solani (J. Agric. Food Chem., 2021)

children.note: Opens the general map on wilt diseases.
Opens the general map on root and collar rots.
Alternaria brown spot, Septoria spot and anthracnose cause leaf spots, stem lesions and sunken fruit spots in warm, wet weather.
Prune for airflow, remove infected parts, avoid overhead irrigation and keep vines well fed. Copper is allowed in organic within limits.
Opens the general map on blights and leaf spots.
Weeds compete for water and nutrients and also harbour aphids and viruses.
Keep a weed-free or mulched strip under the trellis by hand weeding or slashing; avoid deep cultivation that cuts surface roots.
Low cover crops or slashed grass between rows protect the soil and reduce weeding.
Opens the general map on organic weed management.
Fruit for fresh markets must look good, so careful picking and cool storage matter.
Pick purple fruit when fully coloured, or collect ripe fruit that has dropped every day or two. Yellow fruit is often collected after it falls.

manas.q: How do growers know purple passion fruit is ready?

children.note: Clean, sort by size and colour, and pack in ventilated cartons. Remove damaged and fruit-fly-stung fruit.
Passion fruit loses water and wrinkles quickly at room temperature. Cool storage slows wrinkling; wrinkled fruit is still good inside but fetches less.
Small, wrinkled or blemished fruit goes to pulp and juice processing, an important outlet for yellow fruit.
Kenya exports fresh purple passion fruit to Europe and the Middle East; buyers set strict quality and residue rules.
Exporters register with the Horticultural Crops Directorate (AFA-HCD), and KEPHIS inspects consignments. Many buyers also require GLOBALG.A.P.
Importing countries set maximum residue limits for pesticides. Organic growing avoids most residue problems, but drift from neighbours must be prevented.
Exports to the EU need certification under the EU organic regulation; local sales can use PGS or the East African organic standard.
Passion fruit is grown in the Northeast, Kerala and the Nilgiris; NPOP certification is needed for organic exports.

nodeData.note: Mango is a long-lived tropical fruit tree grown from Kenya's coast and Eastern region to all of India. Organic success rests on grafted trees, a low open canopy, timed water, weaver ants and area-wide fruit fly control.

children.note: Mango is a long-lived evergreen tree grown across the tropics and subtropics. Choosing the right variety and grafted planting material decides yield, market and pest pressure for decades.
Mango belongs to the Anacardiaceae, the same family as cashew. It originated in South and Southeast Asia, and India is still the largest producer.

manas.q: To which plant family does mango belong?

children.note: Indian-type mangoes usually have one embryo per seed, so seedlings differ from the parent. Many Southeast Asian types are polyembryonic and give true-to-type seedlings, which makes them useful as uniform rootstocks.

manas.q: Why are polyembryonic mango seeds useful for rootstocks?

children.note: Grafted varieties such as Apple, Ngowe, Kent, Tommy Atkins, Van Dyke and Keitt are widely grown in Kenya. Apple and Ngowe are local favourites; Kent and Tommy Atkins travel well for export and processing.
Alphonso, Kesar, Dasheri, Langra, Banganapalli and Totapuri dominate Indian orchards. TNAU also lists the dwarf hybrids Mallika and Amrapali, suited to closer planting.
Grafted trees start bearing in a few years and keep the variety true. Seedling trees take much longer, vary in quality and grow very tall, which makes spraying, pruning and harvest hard.

manas.q: Why should mango orchards be planted with grafted trees?

children.note: Mango loves heat and a dry spell before flowering. It tolerates poor soils but not waterlogging or frost.
A dry or cool period stops shoot growth and lets flower buds form. Areas with rain during flowering get poor fruit set and heavy anthracnose and powdery mildew.

manas.q: Which weather before flowering helps mango flower well?

children.note: Mango roots go deep, so deep soils with good drainage give long-lived trees. TNAU recommends red loamy soils with a pH of about 6.5–8.0.
Young trees are killed by frost, and strong wind at flowering and fruit set knocks off flowers and fruitlets. Windbreaks help on exposed sites.
A mango orchard is a 30-plus-year investment, so layout, planting material and pits deserve care.
Buy from a registered nursery (KEPHIS-inspected in Kenya) and check the graft union is healthy. Reject plants with black leaf spots, scale insects or malformed shoots.
Cleft or side-veneer grafting of scions onto vigorous local rootstock seedlings is standard. Use scions from healthy, high-yielding mother trees.
TNAU gives 7–10 m between trees for conventional planting and 5 × 5 m (400 trees/ha) for high-density orchards that are kept small by pruning.

manas.q: What spacing does TNAU give for high-density mango?

children.note: Dig large pits weeks before planting and refill with topsoil mixed with well-rotted compost or manure. This is the best moment to add mycorrhiza and other biofertilizers.
Before the canopy closes, legumes, vegetables or pineapple can earn income between rows. Keep them out of the tree basin and avoid tall crops that shade young trees.
Feed the soil with organic matter every year and correct micronutrients. Too much nitrogen gives leafy flushes instead of flowers.

TNAU gives 10 kg farmyard manure per tree in year 1, rising by 10 kg a year to 50 kg from year 6. Organic growers supply the nutrients through compost, manure and legumes instead of the NPK in that schedule.

manas.q: How much FYM per tree does TNAU suggest for a 6-year-old mango tree?

children.note: Main feeding goes on after harvest and pruning to support the new flush that will carry next year's flowers. Avoid heavy nitrogen just before flowering.
A thick mulch of grass, prunings or crop residues keeps the root zone moist and feeds soil life. Keep mulch a hand-width away from the trunk.
Sow legumes such as cowpea, lablab or sunn hemp between rows in the rains and slash them onto the basins. They add nitrogen and organic matter.
Mango often lacks boron (poor fruit set, cracked or deformed fruit) and zinc (small, narrow leaves). Confirm with a leaf test; organic standards allow trace-element salts when a need is shown.
Use microbes as helpers on top of compost, not as a replacement.
Mix mycorrhiza inoculum and a phosphate-solubilising bacteria product into the compost in the planting pit, so they colonise new roots.
Blend Azospirillum, PSB and potassium-mobilising bacteria with compost and spread in the moist basin after harvest. Keep them away from copper sprays.
How mycorrhizal fungi extend tree roots and how to inoculate.
How PSB release locked phosphorus and how to apply them.
Water decides fruit size, but a dry spell is needed for flowering. Timing matters more than quantity.
TNAU advises stopping irrigation for about 30 days before flowering to induce stress, then restarting once flowers appear.

manas.q: When should irrigation be held back in mango?

children.note: Regular water from fruit set to maturity cuts fruit drop and builds size. Drip with mulch is the most efficient.
Easing irrigation in the last weeks before harvest improves sweetness and keeping quality.
Mango flowers on mature shoot tips. Uniform, well-timed flowering gives a crop that can be protected and harvested together.
Shoots need to rest and harden for some months before they can flower. Late flushes after harvest often do not flower that season.
Many varieties give a heavy crop one year and little the next. Moderate crops, timely pruning and good feeding reduce the swing.

manas.q: What is alternate bearing in mango?

children.note: Flies, bees and other insects pollinate mango flowers. Keep flowering weeds and hedges nearby and do not spray at bloom.

Paclobutrazol (a synthetic growth regulator) and potassium nitrate sprays are used conventionally to force flowering. They are not allowed under organic standards; organic growers rely on stress, pruning and timing.

manas.q: Is paclobutrazol allowed in organic mango?

children.note: Protecting bees and flies that set fruit.
A low, open canopy lets light in, cuts disease and makes spraying and harvest easy.
Pinch the young tree at about knee-to-waist height and keep three or four well-spaced main branches. This builds a low, open frame.
Cut back shoots soon after harvest so new flushes have time to mature before the next flowering season.

manas.q: When is the best time to prune mango?

children.note: Remove crossing, dead and inward branches. Sun and air in the canopy dry leaves faster and reduce anthracnose and mildew.
Very tall, old trees can be cut back hard in stages and new shoots trained. They return to bearing in about two to three years.
Fruit flies, seed weevil, scales and hoppers are the main mango pests. Natural enemies, above all weaver ants, do much of the work in organic orchards.
Oriental fruit fly and mango fruit fly (Ceratitis cosyra) lay eggs in ripening fruit; maggots rot the pulp.
Small sting marks with sap, soft patches that spread under the skin, early fruit drop and maggots inside cut fruit.

manas.q: How do you recognise fruit fly damage on mango?

children.note: Collect fallen fruit every few days, use protein bait sprays and male lures, bag fruit, harvest at mature-green and keep weaver ants. Work with neighbours across the area.
Lures, baits, augmentoria and the icipe IPM package.
Sternochetus mangiferae is a weevil whose larva lives inside the seed. It is a quarantine pest for several export markets.
The fruit usually looks normal outside; the seed is eaten and holds the larva or adult. Infested fruits may drop early.

manas.q: Where does the mango seed weevil larva feed?

children.note: Adults hide under loose bark and in cracks between seasons and lay eggs on young fruit. Collect and destroy fallen fruit and seeds, and remove loose bark.

manas.q: How do organic farmers break the seed weevil cycle?

children.note: Other weevils and beetles and their organic control.
Oecophylla ants build leaf nests in the canopy and hunt fruit flies, seed weevils and bugs. A meta-analysis found ants generally reduce pests and plant damage.
Move nests from other trees, link trees with ropes or branches, and protect colonies from broad-spectrum sprays. Control competing ground ants.

manas.q: How can farmers spread weaver ants through a mango orchard?

children.note: Ants leave small dark marks on the skin. A study found these marks did not harm internal quality or storage life of the fruit.
Trials in Benin found fewer fruit fly-damaged mangoes where weaver ants were abundant, and a 2026 Thai study found chemical sprays did not outperform ant biocontrol.
White mango scale is a major pest in Kenya; hoppers and giant mealybug are serious in India. All suck sap and leave honeydew and sooty mould.
Prune infested shoots, band trunks against mealybug crawlers, conserve ladybirds and parasitic wasps, and use horticultural oil or neem when numbers build up.
Scales, mealybugs, hoppers and thrips in detail.
Anthracnose and powdery mildew cause the biggest losses, both linked to wet or humid weather at flowering.
Fungi of the Colletotrichum gloeosporioides group attack leaves, flowers and fruit. It is the most damaging mango disease worldwide.
Black spots on young leaves, blackened flower panicles and dark sunken patches on ripening fruit, often in tear-stain streaks.

manas.q: What does anthracnose look like on ripening mango?

children.note: The fungus enters young fruit in the field and stays dormant, only showing as the fruit ripens. So field control decides post-harvest losses.

manas.q: Why does mango anthracnose often appear only after harvest?

children.note: Prune for airflow, remove dead twigs and old fruit, and protect flowers and young fruit with copper (allowed with limits) or Bacillus biofungicides.
Hot-water treatment of fruit lowers anthracnose in storage. Research on chitosan coatings with plant essential oils is promising.
Anthracnose and other leaf and fruit spots.
A fungus (Erysiphe quercicola, long called Oidium mangiferae) that coats flowers and young fruit with white powder.
White powdery growth on flower stalks, young leaves and fruitlets, followed by browning and heavy flower and fruit drop.

manas.q: Which mango organs does powdery mildew damage most?

children.note: Start at early panicle stage with wettable sulphur or potassium bicarbonate. Bacillus subtilis and other biocontrol agents have shown control in field trials.
How mildews spread and how to manage them organically.
Xanthomonas causes raised black, cracked spots on leaves and fruit, spread by wind-driven rain. Windbreaks, clean planting material and copper help.
Bunchy, deformed flower panicles caused by Fusarium fungi, common in parts of India. Cut out and burn malformed panicles well below the affected part.
Weeds compete most with young trees. Mature trees mainly need a clean basin and short ground cover.
Keep the basin to the drip line weed-free with mulch rather than deep hoeing, which cuts feeder roots.
Slash or graze grass between rows and leave the cuttings as cover. Herbicides are not allowed in organic orchards.
Mulch, cover crops and mechanical weeding.
Most mango losses happen between the tree and the buyer. Careful picking and cool handling protect the price.
Shoulders rise above the stalk, the skin colour softens and the flesh near the seed turns yellow. Mature fruit is denser and sinks in water.

manas.q: Name two signs that a mango is mature for picking.

children.note: Pick by hand or with a padded picking pole, leaving a short stalk. This stops sap from running onto the skin.
The milky sap burns the skin and leaves dark marks. De-sap fruit stalk-down on racks, away from the soil.

manas.q: Why is mango placed stalk-down after picking?

children.note: Keep fruit in the shade in clean crates, never on bare ground. Grade, then cool as soon as possible to slow ripening.
Drying, pulp and juice turn surplus or off-grade fruit into income, as Makueni farmers in Kenya have shown.
Mango sells fresh at home, in regional and Middle East markets, and in Europe for high-quality, residue-free fruit.
Fruit flies and seed weevil decide market access. Interceptions in Europe have in the past led Kenya to suspend mango exports, so area-wide control matters.

manas.q: Which two mango pests most limit exports?

children.note: Exporters must register with the Horticultural Crops Directorate and pass KEPHIS phytosanitary inspection. Buyers often also need GlobalG.A.P.
APEDA runs export registration. Markets such as the USA and Japan require approved treatments like irradiation or vapour-heat for fruit flies.
Importing countries set maximum residue limits for each pesticide. Organic fruit avoids synthetic residues but copper and sulphur rules still apply.
Certification needs a conversion period and records of every input. Groups of smallholders can certify together under an internal control system.
How certification works in Kenya, India and for export.

Step-by-step pruning to keep trees low, open and productive.

children.note: Access Agriculture: picking, de-sapping and handling to avoid damage.
Trusted sources for further study.

Classic review of the disease, its economic impact and integrated control.

Botany, history, varieties and world production.

nodeData.note: Oranges, tangerines (mandarins) and lemons are grafted trees that bear for decades. Organic success rests on clean nursery trees, the right rootstock, good drainage, conserved natural enemies and fast action against greening.

children.note: Citrus covers oranges, mandarins/tangerines, lemons, limes and grapefruit. All are grafted onto a rootstock chosen for the soil and disease risks.
Sweet orange (Citrus sinensis), mandarin or tangerine (C. reticulata), lemon (C. limon), lime and grapefruit are the main types. Many modern varieties are hybrids such as tangelos.

manas.q: What is the botanical name of the sweet orange?

children.note: Valencia and Washington Navel oranges, Minneola tangelo and the seedless Pixie tangerine are popular. Pixie growing has spread fast in Makueni and other dry Eastern counties.
Nagpur mandarin, Kinnow (Punjab), Coorg mandarin, Mosambi sweet orange and Kagzi acid lime are the best-known types. TNAU lists Coorg and Kodai oranges for the hill zones.
Citrus does not ripen further after picking; sugar and flavour stop developing once the fruit is cut. Pick only when it tastes ready.

manas.q: Do oranges ripen after harvest?

children.note: Citrus grows from sea level to cool highlands, but heat, altitude and drainage change fruit quality and disease.
Lowland heat gives sweet fruit but greenish peel; cool nights at higher altitude turn the peel orange. Mandarins in TNAU's hill zones grow at 500–1500 m.

manas.q: Why do oranges from hot lowlands often stay green when ripe?

children.note: Citrus roots die in waterlogged soil and Phytophthora thrives there. Choose deep, free-draining soil or plant on ridges.

manas.q: Which soil condition most favours Phytophthora in citrus?

children.note: TNAU recommends deep loams with pH 5.5–6.5 for mandarin; it also advises lime or dolomite every 2–3 years on acid hill soils.
Most serious citrus diseases arrive with the planting material. Clean trees on the right rootstock are the best investment a grower can make.
Buy from a certified nursery that raises budwood under insect-proof screens. A tree carrying greening or tristeza will never recover.

manas.q: Why must citrus nurseries be insect-screened?

children.note: A bud of the chosen variety is grafted onto a seedling rootstock. Keep the bud union well above the soil to avoid collar infection.
The rootstock gives disease tolerance, vigour and drought or salt tolerance.
The usual rootstock in Kenya and much of India: vigorous and drought-hardy, but prone to Phytophthora and gives larger, less sweet fruit.

manas.q: What is the most common citrus rootstock in Kenya?

children.note: Widely used in India and Brazil for its tolerance of drought and salt. It is sensitive to some graft-transmitted viroids.
Trifoliate orange and its hybrids (Carrizo/Troyer citrange, Swingle citrumelo) tolerate Phytophthora and tristeza but suffer in alkaline, chalky soils.

manas.q: Name a rootstock tolerant of Phytophthora root rot.

children.topic: Avoid sour orange where tristeza occurs
children.note: Sour orange gives good fruit and resists gummosis, but sweet orange on sour orange collapses when tristeza virus is present.
TNAU uses 6 × 6 m with 75 cm pits for mandarin. Fill pits with topsoil and well-rotted compost a few weeks before planting.
Citrus is a heavy feeder for nitrogen and potassium and often short of zinc, magnesium and manganese.
TNAU gives 10 kg FYM per mandarin tree in year 1, rising to 30 kg from year 6, applied in two splits. Organic growers meet the NPK part with compost, manure and legumes.

manas.q: How much FYM does TNAU suggest per mature mandarin tree?

children.note: Feeder roots lie under the outer canopy, so spread compost in a ring under the drip line, not against the trunk.

children.topic: Mulch, but not at the collar
children.note: Mulch keeps roots cool and moist, but keep it clear of the trunk; wet mulch at the collar invites gummosis.
Zinc lack gives small, narrow, mottled leaves; magnesium lack gives an inverted yellow V on older leaves. Organic standards allow trace-element salts when a test shows the need.

manas.q: What does magnesium deficiency look like on citrus leaves?

children.note: Sow cowpea, lablab or sunn hemp between rows and slash them for mulch, adding nitrogen and organic matter.
Microbes help roots take up nutrients; use them with compost.
Citrus roots have few root hairs and depend heavily on mycorrhizal fungi. TNAU advises 1 kg mycorrhiza inoculum per mature mandarin tree.

manas.q: Why does citrus benefit so much from mycorrhiza?

children.note: Mix with compost and apply into moist soil under the canopy after harvest. Keep apart from copper sprays.
Adding Trichoderma-enriched compost at planting helps protect young roots against soil pathogens.
Inoculation methods and how to see mycorrhiza working.
Citrus needs steady moisture for fruit set and size, but its roots hate wet feet.
Flowering, fruit set and fruit growth are the stages where drought causes fruit drop and small fruit.

manas.q: At which stages is water stress most harmful to citrus?

children.note: In the tropics, a dry spell followed by irrigation triggers a flush of flowers. Indian growers time this to choose the crop season (bahar).
Drip saves water and keeps the trunk dry. Never let water stand against the trunk, which favours gummosis.
Psyllids, false codling moth, scales, fruit flies and leaf miner are the main pests. Conserving natural enemies is the backbone of organic control.
Psyllids are tiny sap-sucking bugs that spread greening. Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri) and African citrus psyllid (Trioza erytreae) both occur in East Africa.
Young shoots twist and curl; African psyllid nymphs make pimple-like pits on leaves; Asian psyllid nymphs leave white waxy threads.

manas.q: What do African citrus psyllid nymphs do to leaves?

children.note: The Asian citrus psyllid was found in Tanzania in 2014–15 surveys and in Kenya soon after, raising the risk of the Asian form of greening.

manas.q: Which invasive citrus psyllid was recently found in Kenya?

children.note: Check new flushes weekly, prune off infested shoots, use yellow sticky traps, and spray neem or horticultural oil on flushes when psyllids are found.
The parasitic wasp Tamarixia radiata attacks Asian psyllid nymphs and has been released in Florida and California.
Psyllids, aphids, scales and mites in detail.
Thaumatotibia leucotreta, an African moth whose caterpillar bores into citrus, avocado and many other fruits.
A small hole with brown frass and a yellow-brown patch on the peel; infested fruit colours early and drops.

manas.q: What are the signs of false codling moth on an orange?

children.note: The EU treats FCM as a quarantine pest, so a single live larva can block a consignment. South Africa uses a systems approach to meet this.
Pick up and destroy dropped fruit twice a week, monitor with pheromone traps, and use mating disruption, the FCM granulovirus (CrleGV) and egg parasitoids.

manas.q: Name a virus used as a biopesticide against false codling moth.

children.note: Entomopathogenic nematodes from citrus orchards kill FCM larvae and pupae in the soil under trees.
Bt, viruses, pheromones and other caterpillar controls.
Red scale (armoured) and soft scales suck sap; soft scales and mealybugs make honeydew and sooty mould.
Crusty or waxy bumps on twigs, leaves and fruit, yellow spots under them, sticky leaves and black sooty mould.

manas.q: Which scale insects produce sticky honeydew?

children.note: Aphytis and other tiny wasps and ladybirds (Chilocorus) keep scales low when not killed by broad-spectrum sprays.
Ants farm soft scales and chase away their enemies. Sticky bands or barriers on trunks let natural enemies work.

manas.q: Why does controlling ants reduce scale problems?

children.note: Horticultural mineral oil, allowed in organic, smothers young scales. Aim at the crawler stage and avoid spraying in hot midday sun.
Fruit flies attack ripening fruit, especially mandarins; leaf miner larvae tunnel young leaves and open entry for canker.
Baits, lures and orchard sanitation.
Greening is the deadliest citrus disease; Phytophthora is the commonest killer of young and waterlogged trees.
Huanglongbing is caused by phloem bacteria (Candidatus Liberibacter species) spread by psyllids and infected budwood. There is no cure.
Blotchy, uneven yellow mottling not matching across the midrib, yellow shoots, small lopsided bitter fruit that stay green at the bottom, and aborted seeds.

manas.q: How does greening leaf mottle differ from nutrient deficiency?

children.note: Asian (Ca. L. asiaticus) is spread by the Asian psyllid; African (Ca. L. africanus) by the African citrus psyllid, which favours cool highlands.

manas.q: Which psyllid spreads African greening?

children.note: Plant clean nursery trees, control psyllids on new flushes, remove infected trees quickly and work with neighbours. Good nutrition and root health help trees cope.
Greening, canker and other bacterial diseases.
Water moulds (Phytophthora nicotianae, P. citrophthora) rot the bark at the collar and the feeder roots.
Gum oozing from cracked bark near the soil, dead brown bark under it, yellowing canopy and dieback; fruit near the ground gets brown rot.

manas.q: What is the first visible sign of citrus gummosis?

children.note: Use tolerant rootstocks, plant high with the bud union above soil, avoid wounds and water against the trunk, and improve drainage.
Scrape away diseased bark to healthy tissue and paint with Bordeaux paste; apply Trichoderma-enriched compost under the canopy. Biocontrol fungi have shown promise in trials.
Metalaxyl/mefenoxam and phosphonate fungicides used conventionally are not permitted under organic standards.

manas.q: Are phosphonates allowed for Phytophthora control in organic citrus?

children.note: Phytophthora and other root diseases.
Citrus tristeza virus spreads with aphids and budwood; trees on sour orange decline quickly. Use tolerant rootstocks and clean budwood.
How plant viruses spread and are managed.
Citrus black spot (a fungus) blemishes fruit and is an EU quarantine disease; citrus canker (a bacterium) causes raised corky spots. Copper, with limits, and sanitation help.
A clean, mulched basin and slashed ground cover between rows keep weeds in check.
Citrus feeder roots are near the surface, so deep hoeing damages them and opens the way for root rot. Mulch and hand-pull instead.

manas.q: Why should deep hoeing be avoided under citrus?

children.note: Slash grass or legumes between rows. Flowering cover also feeds the parasitoids and predators that control citrus pests.
Mulch, cover crops and mechanical weeding.
Good picking and handling keep citrus sound for weeks; rough handling causes rots and peel damage.
Harvest when the sugar-to-acid balance is right for the market, not by colour alone, since warm-area fruit stays green.
Cut the stem close to the fruit with clippers. Pulling tears the peel, and long stems puncture other fruit.

manas.q: Why should citrus be clipped rather than pulled?

children.note: Turgid fruit picked wet or early in the morning bruises easily, releasing peel oil that leaves dark spots. Pick dry fruit.
Pack in clean ventilated crates and keep cool. Synthetic post-harvest fungicides and waxes are not permitted in organic packing.
Citrus sells fresh and for juice. Export markets are strict on quarantine pests and residues.
Kenya imports many oranges, so local fresh-fruit and juice markets are open for good quality. Pixies sell well in Nairobi and Mombasa.
The EU sets strict rules for citrus imports on FCM, black spot and greening. Fruit must come from registered, inspected orchards.
Buyers check pesticide residues against limits. Organic fruit avoids synthetic residues but must still meet copper limits.
In Kenya, KEPHIS inspects and the Horticultural Crops Directorate registers exporters. In India, APEDA oversees exports and NPOP organic certification.
How to certify, alone or as a group.
Practical videos on citrus health and organic pest control.
University of Florida: what HLB is, how it spreads and why it matters.

children.note: Entomological Society of America: finding eggs, nymphs and adults on flush.
Kenyan report on biological options against FCM.
NSW Agriculture: beneficial insects that keep citrus pests down.
NSW Agriculture: monitoring and biological control of soft scale.
