nodeData.note: A field guide to growing arabica coffee organically, with a focus on Kenya: resistant varieties, shade, mulching and pulp compost, and organic answers to berry borer, Antestia, CBD and leaf rust.

children.note: Arabica coffee (Coffea arabica) is a self-pollinating evergreen shrub from the Ethiopian highlands; robusta (C. canephora) is a lowland species. Kenya grows almost only arabica, mostly on small farms organised in cooperatives.
Arabica grows at higher, cooler altitudes and gives the finer cup; robusta tolerates heat and lowlands, has more caffeine and a harsher taste. India grows both, Uganda mainly robusta.

manas.q: Which coffee species does Kenya mainly grow?

children.note: Tall Kenyan selections made by Scott Agricultural Laboratories in the 1930s. They give Kenya's famous bright, fruity cup, but both are susceptible to coffee berry disease and leaf rust.

manas.q: What is the main weakness of SL28 and SL34?

children.note: A compact hybrid released by Kenya's Coffee Research Institute in 1985, resistant to coffee berry disease and leaf rust. Its short stature allows closer spacing than the tall SL types.

manas.q: When was Ruiru 11 released and what does it resist?

children.note: A tall, true-breeding variety released in 2010, resistant to CBD and leaf rust, with a cup quality close to SL28. Seed can be saved from it, unlike the Ruiru 11 hybrid.

manas.q: Name the tall Kenyan variety released in 2010 that resists CBD and rust.

children.note: Old SL trees can be top-worked: Ruiru 11 or Batian scions are grafted onto new suckers, so the farmer keeps the old root system while gaining disease resistance. This sharply cuts the need for copper sprays.

manas.q: How can a farmer convert old SL28 trees to a resistant variety without uprooting?

children.note: India's Coffee Board and the Central Coffee Research Institute (Chikmagalur) breed arabica and robusta selections for Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, mostly grown under two-tier shade.
Arabica needs mild temperatures, well-spread rain with a short dry spell to trigger flowering, and deep, well-drained, slightly acid soil rich in organic matter.
In Kenya arabica is grown roughly between 1,400 and 2,100 m around Mt Kenya, the Aberdares, Kisii, Mt Elgon and Kericho/Nandi. Heat above about 30 °C stresses arabica and favours berry borer.

manas.q: Why is heat bad for arabica beyond plant stress?

children.note: Kenya's two rainy seasons give two flowerings and so a main and a fly crop. Flowers open a week or so after rain that ends a dry spell.
Deep red volcanic soils, slightly acid, well drained and full of organic matter suit coffee best. Waterlogged or shallow soils lead to root rots and dieback.
Warming is pushing arabica's ideal zone uphill and lets berry borer breed more often; shade trees are the main on-farm adaptation suggested by East African studies.
A coffee farm stays productive for decades, so time spent on clean seedlings, good holes and shade planning pays back for years.
Buy seed or seedlings of Ruiru 11 or Batian from certified sources (Coffee Research Institute or licensed nurseries). Home-raised Ruiru 11 seed does not breed true.

manas.q: Why should Ruiru 11 seed not be saved on-farm?

children.note: Raise seedlings in polybags of topsoil, sand and well-matured compost, under 50% shade, with clean water. Mycorrhiza and Trichoderma added to the mix give healthier roots.
Dig holes well ahead of the rains, keep topsoil and subsoil apart, and refill with topsoil mixed with plenty of mature manure or compost. Plant at the start of the long rains.
Plant shade trees such as Grevillea, Cordia africana or Albizia before or with the coffee, so they are useful when the bushes start bearing.
On slopes make terraces or contour bunds and grass strips (such as Napier) before planting to stop erosion of the topsoil.

Coffee removes nitrogen and potassium in the largest amounts, mostly in cherries and prunings. An organic plan returns these through compost, pulp, prunings, manure and legumes, with biofertilizers to unlock soil nutrients.
Each crop exports N, K, P, Ca and Mg in the cherries. Leaves and prunings left in the field recycle a large share; pulp sent back from the factory returns much of the rest.

manas.q: Which two nutrients does coffee remove in the largest amounts?

children.note: Pale yellow older leaves suggest nitrogen shortage; scorched leaf edges and poor berry filling suggest potassium; small, narrow, crowded leaves at shoot tips suggest zinc.
Pulp from wet processing is rich in potassium and organic matter. Compost it in heaps mixed with manure and dry material, turning until it no longer smells sour, before spreading under bushes.

manas.q: Which nutrient is coffee pulp especially rich in?

children.note: Earthworms such as Eudrilus eugeniae can turn coffee pulp into a fine vermicompost; trials in Colombia and India found it a better product than simple turned piles.

links.label: 📄 Source: Biology and Fertility of Soils 1996

children.note: Spread well-rotted cattle or goat manure in a ring under the drip line at the start of the rains, then cover with mulch. Never pile fresh manure against the stem.
Leguminous shade trees, Desmodium or beans between young rows, and lopped Calliandra or Leucaena leaves add nitrogen and organic matter.

Nursery: mycorrhiza and Trichoderma in the potting mix. Planting: the same in the hole with compost. Mature bushes: Azotobacter or Azospirillum, PSB and KMB mixed into compost and applied at the onset of rains.

manas.q: Which biofertilizers suit the coffee nursery mix?

children.note: Very acid soils can be corrected with agricultural lime or dolomite, which are allowed in organic farming; rock phosphate supplies slow phosphorus. Base decisions on a soil test.
Synthetic fertilizers such as CAN, urea or NPK compounds are not permitted on certified organic coffee.
Coffee roots are shallow, so keeping the topsoil cool and moist through the dry season decides next year's crop.
A thick mulch of dry grass, maize stover or prunings keeps soil moist and cool, feeds soil life and smothers weeds. Keep it a hand's width away from the stem.

manas.q: Why keep mulch away from the coffee stem?

children.note: Moderate shade buffers heat, slows weeds and drops leaf litter. Too much shade lowers yield and keeps leaves wet, so lop shade trees before the rains.

manas.q: What happens when coffee is over-shaded?

children.note: A Brazilian study found shade trees changed soil nutrients and soil fauna more strongly on organic than on conventional coffee farms.

links.label: 📄 Source: Science of the Total Environment 2019

children.note: In robusta farms of Kodagu, India, farms with more kinds of shade trees had higher yields, bigger beans and less berry borer than farms dominated by one tree species.

manas.q: What did the Kodagu study find about diverse shade?

children.note: Where irrigation exists, a single watering after a long dry spell can produce an even flowering; drip and basin irrigation save water.
Pruning keeps bushes open, light and productive, and removes the wood where pests and diseases build up.
Kenyan farmers train SL and Batian bushes on one to three upright stems (capped multiple-stem system); remove excess suckers regularly.
Remove dead, crossing and inward-growing branches after harvest so light and air reach the centre; this cuts rust, CBD and berry borer habitat.

manas.q: How does pruning help against coffee diseases?

children.note: Unproductive bushes can be cut low to regrow new stems; plan it after harvest and keep the stumps mulched and fed.
The pests that matter most in Kenya are the coffee berry borer, Antestia bugs, leaf miners, thrips, mealybugs, scales and stem borers.
Hypothenemus hampei is a tiny black beetle, the world's worst coffee pest. The female bores a hole at the tip (navel) of the berry and breeds inside the bean.

manas.q: Where on the berry does the berry borer enter?

children.note: A neat pinhole at the berry tip, sometimes with fine dust; bored green berries drop, and bored beans are hollowed and lose weight and grade.
The beetle develops faster in warm conditions, so it is spreading to higher coffee zones as temperatures rise.
Clean harvesting (pick all ripe, overripe and fallen berries; strip at season end), Beauveria bassiana sprays, alcohol-baited traps and African parasitoid wasps. Shade with diverse trees helps.

manas.q: What is the key cultural control for berry borer?

children.note: Opens the beetles map for biology and organic control of borers and weevils.
Antestiopsis species are shield bugs with orange, black and white markings. They suck buds, flowers and green berries.

manas.q: What do Antestia bugs look like?

children.note: Flower buds blacken and drop, berries fall, beans inside show zebra-like brown streaks, and shoots become bushy with many small branches (fan branching).
Antestia feeding is linked to 'potato taste' defect in East African coffee, which spoils whole lots at cupping.

manas.q: Which cup defect is linked to Antestia bugs?

children.note: Unlike most coffee pests, Antestia is most numerous at higher, cooler elevations and in the cool dry season.
Prune to open the bush, hand-pick and shake bugs onto a sheet early in the morning, and use pyrethrum (natural, organic-allowed) only where counts are high.
Opens the sucking pests map: bugs, mealybugs, scales, thrips and mites.

Leaf miner caterpillars make brown blotch mines on upper leaves; thrips cause silvery, scarred leaves in hot dry spells. Natural enemies usually keep both in check if broad-spectrum sprays are avoided.
These suck sap at berry clusters and shoots and are farmed by ants for honeydew. Band stems with sticky grease to keep ants off, and natural enemies will usually clean them up.
A longhorn beetle larva rings the bark near the ground and tunnels in the stem, often killing young bushes. Check stems for frass, kill larvae with a wire and keep the base clean.
Coffee berry disease and leaf rust are the two big fungal diseases in Kenya; root rots and wilt matter locally.
Colletotrichum kahawae attacks green, expanding berries. It is found only in Africa and can destroy most of a crop on susceptible varieties in wet years.

manas.q: Which coffee stage does CBD attack?

children.note: Small dark sunken spots on green berries that spread and blacken the berry; dead berries stay mummified on the branch and carry spores to the next season.
Spores splash in rain and drip from mummified berries and bark; cool wet weather during berry expansion is the danger period, worst at high altitude.
In Cameroon, shaded coffee had less CBD than coffee in full sun; shade changed the microclimate rather than the berries' own susceptibility.

manas.q: How does shade reduce CBD?

children.note: Plant Ruiru 11 or Batian or graft them; prune and remove mummified berries; time copper sprays (allowed with limits) to the main berry expansion rains.
Opens the blights map with CBD and other wet-weather diseases.
Hemileia vastatrix causes yellow-orange powdery spots on the underside of leaves and heavy leaf fall; it is worse at lower, warmer altitudes.

manas.q: Where on the leaf is the orange rust powder?

children.note: Resistant varieties first; then balanced organic feeding, open pruning, moderate shade and copper protectant sprays before the rains.
In a Mexican shaded farm, outbreaks of the fungus Lecanicillium lecanii on green scales were followed a year later by lower rust levels.
Opens the mildews and rusts map.

Armillaria root rot kills bushes planted on land cleared from forest; coffee wilt (Fusarium xylarioides) is serious in Uganda and DRC. Remove dead bushes with their roots and do not move planting material from wilt areas.
Root-knot and lesion nematodes cause stunting and yellowing, worst in nurseries on reused soil. Use clean nursery soil and compost-rich planting holes.
Weeds compete hardest with young coffee and in dry spells, especially couch grass and other perennial grasses.
Mulch, leguminous covers and shade keep weeds down; slash or hand-weed rings around young bushes.
Deep hoeing cuts coffee's shallow feeding roots; shallow weeding or slashing is safer. Herbicides are not allowed in organic coffee.

manas.q: Why avoid deep hoeing under coffee?

children.note: Quality is made at picking and at the factory: only ripe red cherries, processed the same day, give Kenya's top grades.
Pick only fully ripe red cherries every one to two weeks; sort out green, dry and bored berries before delivery.

manas.q: Which cherries should be picked for top quality?

children.note: Kenyan factories pulp, ferment, wash, soak and sun-dry parchment on raised tables. Clean water and careful drying protect the cup.
Pulp should go back to farms as compost, and wastewater should settle in lagoons or soak pits, not run into rivers, where it kills aquatic life.
Store dry parchment in clean bags on pallets, away from smoke, fuel and chemicals that taint coffee.
Kenyan coffee is sold through the Nairobi Coffee Exchange or by direct sales; organic and other certifications can open specialty markets.
About 70% of Kenyan coffee comes from smallholders, mostly through cooperative factories; production has fallen from its 1980s peak.
Exports must meet the buyer's standard (EU organic, USDA NOP, or Japan's JAS); group certification with an internal control system lets cooperatives certify many smallholders together.
Importing countries set maximum residue limits on coffee; organic lots are tested and any synthetic pesticide residue can cost the certificate.
Selected videos from FAO, extension services, coffee boards and an experienced Kenyan grower.
FAO — farmer methods to control berry borer without the banned insecticide.

Coffee Board of India via the International Coffee Organization — recognising and managing rust.

nodeData.note: A field guide to growing tea organically, focused on Kenyan smallholders (KTDA) with notes from India: clones, pruning and plucking, organic nutrition that stops soil acidification, biofertilizers, and organic control of mites and root rots.

children.note: Tea (Camellia sinensis) is an evergreen shrub kept as a flat-topped bush and plucked for its young shoots. Kenya, India, China and Sri Lanka are leading producers; Kenya is among the top black-tea exporters.
The China type (var. sinensis) is small-leaved and cold-tolerant; the Assam type (var. assamica) is large-leaved and high-yielding. Kenyan clones are mostly Assam-type.

manas.q: Which tea type are most Kenyan clones based on?

children.note: Tea came to Limuru in 1903 and estates began in 1924. Most Kenyan tea is CTC black tea for blends, plus some orthodox, green and purple tea.

manas.q: Where and when was tea first planted in Kenya?

children.note: The Kenya Tea Development Agency serves over half a million smallholders with extension, leaf collection, factories and marketing; they produce more than 60% of Kenya's tea.

manas.q: Roughly what share of Kenyan tea do KTDA smallholders produce?

children.note: The Tea Research Institute (KALRO-TRI, Kericho; formerly TRFK) has released many clones for yield, quality and drought tolerance, including purple-leaved tea rich in anthocyanins.

manas.q: Which institute breeds Kenyan tea clones?

children.note: Tocklai Tea Research Institute (Assam) and UPASI (south India) release clones and guidance; Darjeeling, Assam and the Nilgiris have certified organic gardens.
Tea needs plenty of well-spread rain, mild temperatures and deep, well-drained, strongly acid soil.
Kenya's tea zones on both sides of the Rift Valley receive about 1,200–1,400 mm of well-distributed rain on deep red volcanic soils at high altitude.
Tea grows best at soil pH about 4.5–5.5; in a Chinese national survey almost half of tea soils had fallen below 4.5, too acid for good growth.

manas.q: What soil pH range is best for tea?

links.label: 📄 Source: Science of the Total Environment 2020

children.note: Heavy nitrogen fertilizer is the main cause of acidification in tea gardens; long-term trials show pH falling as N doses rise.

manas.q: What is the main cause of soil acidification in tea gardens?

children.note: The same Chinese survey found no significant acidification on organic tea plantations, unlike gardens on chemical fertilizer.

links.label: 📄 Source: Science of the Total Environment 2020

children.note: Ground frost in high valleys and long dry spells in the east of the Rift scorch shoots; shade trees, mulch and drought-tolerant clones reduce damage.
Tea lives for many decades, so clean land, good cuttings and a strong first frame decide the garden's future.
Old tree stumps and roots carry Armillaria root rot. Ring-bark trees a year or more before felling and remove stumps and large roots before planting.

manas.q: Why ring-bark trees before clearing land for tea?

children.note: Tea is propagated from one-leaf, one-node cuttings of a chosen clone, rooted in sleeves of acid subsoil under shade and high humidity for several months.

manas.q: How are tea plants usually propagated?

children.note: Use acid, weed-free subsoil for rooting; avoid lime, ash and fresh manure, which raise pH and burn cuttings. Clean soil avoids nematodes.
Mycorrhizal fungi changed root system architecture and boosted growth of tea cuttings in pot trials, so adding AMF inoculum to nursery soil is promising.
Plant hardened plants at the start of the rains in holes enriched with mature compost; contour rows and grass strips protect slopes from erosion.
Young plants are pegged or tipped to form a wide, low frame that becomes the flat plucking table.
Tea removes a lot of nitrogen in every flush of plucked shoots. Organic gardens return it through compost, manure, prunings, oil cakes and legumes, and keep the soil from acidifying.
Every plucking round carries away young shoots rich in nitrogen and potassium, so nitrogen is the nutrient most often limiting tea yields.

manas.q: Which nutrient most often limits tea yield?

children.note: Nitrogen: pale small leaves and slow flushing. Potassium: scorched leaf margins and dieback. Magnesium: yellow patches between veins on mature leaves. Zinc: small, narrow, sickle-shaped leaves.
Pruning litter is a huge nutrient bank; leaving it as mulch returns nutrients and organic matter instead of burning or selling it as firewood.

manas.q: Why should tea prunings stay in the garden?

children.note: Apply mature compost or cattle manure between rows at the start of the rains and cover with mulch. In a 4-year trial organic-only plots kept pH 5.1–5.3 while chemical plots fell below 3.
Seed cakes such as rapeseed, neem or castor cake are concentrated organic N sources; rapeseed cake buffered acidification and cut N runoff in a Chinese tea trial.

children.note: Tea gardens managed long-term with organic fertilizer had better rhizosphere soil properties than those on chemical fertilizer in a long-term field study.
Leguminous shade and hedge trees and cover crops in young tea add nitrogen and leaf litter; lop them regularly so they do not over-shade.

manas.q: Name one way legumes add N to a tea garden.

children.note: Nursery: mycorrhiza and Trichoderma in the sleeve soil. Field: Azospirillum, a P solubiliser, mycorrhiza and a K mobiliser mixed with compost after pruning and at the onset of rains.

manas.q: Which biofertilizer package does TNAU suggest for tea?

children.note: Only where pH has fallen far below 4.5 should small doses of dolomite be used, guided by a soil test; liming tea like a maize field harms it.
Synthetic NPK fertilizers such as the compound blends supplied to many smallholders are not permitted on certified organic tea.
Tea is mostly rain-fed; keeping soil covered and partly shaded carries bushes through dry spells.
Mulch young tea heavily with grass or prunings to keep soil cool and moist and to stop erosion until the canopy closes.

manas.q: Why mulch young tea?

children.note: Scattered shade trees such as Grevillea reduce heat and drought stress, add leaf litter and give firewood and timber income.
Where available, irrigation of nurseries and young tea in the dry season prevents losses; most mature smallholder tea is rain-fed.
Pruning keeps the bush at a comfortable plucking height and renews the frame; regular plucking keeps it flushing.
Over years the plucking table rises and gets knotty and less productive; pruning brings it down and renews vigorous shoots.

manas.q: Why do tea bushes need periodic pruning?

children.note: Kenyan bushes are usually pruned every few years, at the end of the rains or in a cool period, never during drought stress.
Leaving a few branches unpruned ('lungs') helps the bush recover faster, especially in drier areas.

manas.q: What are the lung branches in tea pruning?

children.note: New shoots are tipped at an even height to form a level plucking table before regular plucking resumes.
Pluck two leaves and a bud at regular rounds of about one to two weeks; coarse plucking lowers quality and price.

manas.q: What is the standard fine plucking unit for tea?

children.note: Mites, thrips and sucking bugs are the main tea pests; most are kept down by natural enemies when broad-spectrum sprays are avoided.
Oligonychus coffeae turns mature leaves bronze-red on the upper surface in hot dry weather, with fine webbing. Predatory mites and rains bring it down.

manas.q: What weather favours red spider mite in tea?

children.note: Keep bushes well fed and mulched, avoid dust on leaves, conserve predatory mites and ladybirds, and use sulphur or neem only on hot spots.
Opens the sucking pests map: mites, thrips, aphids and bugs.
Tiny insects that scar young leaves, leaving silvery or brown streaks on both sides of the midrib, worst in dry spells. Regular plucking removes many eggs and larvae.
Helopeltis species (a major pest in India) suck young shoots, leaving dark sunken spots that make shoots shrivel. Prune and pluck infested shoots and use neem or Beauveria where severe.
Termites attack drought-stressed or wounded bushes; lesion and root-knot nematodes stunt young tea. Use clean nursery soil and compost-rich planting holes.
Natural enemies, entomopathogenic fungi and botanicals form the base of pest control in organic tea; India's tea research body promotes them widely.
Root rots are the main killers in Kenyan tea; in Asia the leaf disease blister blight is the biggest threat.
Armillaria fungi spread from old forest stumps along roots and kill bushes in patches. White fan-shaped fungal sheets lie under the bark at the collar.

manas.q: What sign under the bark identifies Armillaria root rot?

children.note: Dig out dead bushes with all roots and stumps; leave the ground fallow or under grass before replanting; ring-bark trees long before clearing.

manas.q: What must be removed when a tea bush dies of Armillaria?

children.note: Pseudomonas strains induced defence enzymes in tea against brown root rot and charcoal stump rot in experiments; Trichoderma is also used in compost around replants.
Opens the root rots map.
A wood-decaying fungus in Kenyan tea that enters through pruning cuts and stressed stems; branches die back. Prune cleanly in good weather and keep bushes vigorous.
Exobasidium vexans makes pale, translucent spots on young leaves that bulge into white blisters underneath; it is serious in India and Sri Lanka in misty monsoon weather.

manas.q: Which tea disease causes white blisters under young leaves?

children.note: Sunlight, especially its UV-B part, reduces blister blight; lopping shade during the monsoon helps.
Weekly foliar Pseudomonas fluorescens reduced blister blight almost as well as a chemical fungicide in Indian field trials; copper is the organic fallback.

manas.q: Which bacterium controlled blister blight in Indian tea trials?

children.note: A leaf-surface bacterium from tea also suppressed grey and blister blight in field tests, an area still under research.

Weeds compete hardest in young tea before the canopy closes; mature tea shades most weeds out.
Mulch and careful hand weeding or slashing in young tea; avoid deep digging that cuts feeder roots and causes erosion.
Low cover crops or Guatemala grass mulch between young rows hold soil; herbicides are not allowed in organic tea.

manas.q: Are herbicides allowed in organic tea?

children.note: Green leaf starts to wilt and lose quality the moment it is plucked, so care in handling decides price.
Carry leaf in clean, airy baskets, keep it in shade and deliver to the buying centre quickly; never pack it in plastic or let it heat up.

manas.q: Why should plucked tea leaf never be packed tightly in plastic?

children.note: Factories wither, cut (CTC) or roll, ferment, dry and grade the leaf; about 4 kg of green leaf makes 1 kg of made tea.

manas.q: About how much green leaf makes 1 kg of made tea?

children.note: Smoke from firewood dryers and plastics can leave contaminants that exceed buyer limits; organic factories must keep organic leaf separate.
Most Kenyan tea is sold at the Mombasa auction; organic, Rainforest Alliance and Fairtrade lots reach specialty buyers.
A garden must be managed organically for a conversion period before its tea can be sold as organic; group certification lets smallholders certify together.
The EU and other importers set strict maximum residue limits for tea, which is brewed and drunk without washing; organic leaf is tested for residues.

manas.q: Why are residue limits on tea especially strict?
